scan.summary: This is the company's own written emergency action plan for the Portland facility. It covers alarms, evacuation, shelter-in-place, headcounts, first aid, and training and review. Because it is your document and not an agency's, you can fix it. It covers most of what Oregon OSHA's emergency action plan rule asks for, but it leaves out how to report an emergency, who to contact about the plan, and a clear procedure for shutting down critical equipment. It was last revised in February 2021, even though it says it is reviewed every January.
scan.freshness_note: The revision date is about five years and seven months old. Section 6 says the facilities lead 'reviews the plan every January', but nothing in the file shows a review in 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 or 2026. Ask the facilities lead whether there is a newer version or a signed record of those January reviews. If not, review the plan now and re-date it. The 42 headcount, the exits, and the warden and first-aid names may have changed since 2021.

gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
gaps.description: The plan mentions manual pull stations and says an outside company monitors the alarm. It never tells employees how to report an emergency: who calls 911, what to say, how to report a chemical spill or medical emergency that does not set off the fire alarm, or who tells the incident coordinator. The Oregon rule lists reporting procedures as a required element.
gaps.fix: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section. Cover pulling the nearest station for fire, calling 911 from a safe phone (and whether an outside line needs a dial prefix), who to notify inside the company (the incident coordinator by job title), and how to report spills and medical emergencies. The monitoring company does not replace a 911 call for non-fire events.
gaps.locator: not in the document. Best placed as a new section between Section 2 (Alarm system) and Section 3 (Evacuation procedures).
gaps.quote: Manual pull stations are located at each exit door.

gaps.title: No names or job titles of people to contact about the plan
gaps.description: The rule requires the names or job titles of the people employees can contact for more information about the plan or their duties under it. The plan mentions a 'facilities lead', an 'incident coordinator', floor wardens and a receptionist, but it never names a contact for questions. It also never says which job title serves as incident coordinator.
gaps.fix: Add a contacts section. Name the plan owner (probably the facilities lead) and say who serves as incident coordinator and their alternate, by name or job title, with phone numbers. Point to Appendix B for the warden and first-aid roster.
gaps.locator: not in the document. Could go in Section 1 or a new final section.
gaps.quote: Any person unaccounted for is reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point

gaps.title: Shutdown of critical equipment before evacuation is not set out
gaps.description: The rule requires procedures for anyone who runs or shuts down critical equipment before evacuating. The plan tells everyone to 'secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds'. It covers turning off the ventilation only for shelter-in-place. It does not say whether anything in the lab, warehouse, transfer or dock operations (for example chemical transfers, pumps, lab fume hoods or heating equipment, or forklift charging) must be shut down during an evacuation, or who does it and when that person leaves. It may be that nothing needs to stay running, but then the plan should say so plainly.
gaps.fix: Either state that no employee stays behind to run or shut down equipment during an evacuation, or list each item that needs it, who is assigned (by job title), the steps, and when that person must leave.
gaps.quote: all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit

gaps.title: Plan does not say whether employees respond to chemical spills
gaps.description: The plan covers a 'chemical release' through evacuation and shelter-in-place. It never says whether any employee cleans up or contains spills beyond small ones near the work area. For a chemical distributor, that choice decides whether an emergency action plan is enough or whether a full hazardous substance emergency response plan and training under the federal HAZWOPER rule are needed. That rule is 29 CFR 1910.120(q), which I believe Oregon adopts by reference; I have not checked the exact Oregon rule number.
gaps.fix: Add a sentence stating the company's policy. For example: employees evacuate and outside responders handle releases, and employees only clean up small spills in their own area using the SDS and spill kit. If employees do respond to larger releases, a separate emergency response plan and the related training are needed.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.120(q)(1) (belief, not checked against the Oregon adoption)
gaps.locator: not in the document. Best placed in Section 1 or Section 3.
gaps.quote: For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place signal sounds.

gaps.title: Annual January review not shown
gaps.description: The plan commits to a review every January, but the only date on it is February 2021. The rule requires review when the plan changes or an employee's duties change, not every year. Still, the company's own commitment is not visibly being met, and details like the headcount and roster may be out of date.
gaps.fix: Review the plan now, update the revision date, and add a review log (date, reviewer, changes) to the front page.
gaps.locator: Section 6, Training and review (page 5), and the cover (page 1)
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January

gaps.title: Appendices A and B not in the file
gaps.description: The plan points to evacuation maps (Appendix A) and a warden and first-aid roster (Appendix B). Neither is in this file. The exit-route assignments partly depend on the maps.
gaps.fix: Attach the current maps and roster to the file copy, or upload them separately with their own dates.
gaps.quote: Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
